content_html:
Position sizing answers one question before you place a trade: how many shares can I buy so that, if the stop-loss is hit, I lose only the amount I decided in advance? This calculator uses the fixed-fractional method. You choose a small percentage of your account to risk, set an entry and a stop-loss, and it works out the share count that keeps the loss at the stop within that limit, including trading costs.

How to use this calculator

  1. Account size: the total value of the trading account the position comes from.
  2. Risk per trade: the share of the account you are prepared to lose if the trade fails. Many traders keep this between 0.5% and 2%.
  3. Trade direction: long if you are buying and your stop sits below the entry, short if you are selling short and your stop sits above it.
  4. Entry and stop-loss prices: where you plan to get in and where you will get out if the trade goes against you.
  5. Profit target (optional): the price where you plan to take profits, used to show the reward-to-risk ratio.
  6. More options: a cap on how much of the account any one position may use, and your round-trip trading costs.

How the share count is worked out

First the calculator finds your risk budget: account size times the risk percentage. Then it finds the risk on each share, which is the gap between the entry and the stop-loss. Round-trip costs are taken out of the budget, and what is left is divided by the risk per share and rounded down to whole shares:

shares = floor((account × risk% − costs) ÷ |entry − stop|)

A second limit then applies. If buying that many shares would make the position larger than your maximum position size, the share count is cut to floor(account × max% ÷ entry). The results show which of the two limits decided the size. Rounding down means the actual loss at the stop is usually a little under your budget, never over it.

Worked example

With a $100,000 account and 1% risk, the risk budget is $1,000. Buying at $50 with a stop at $45 puts $5 at risk per share. After $5 of round-trip costs, $995 remains, and $995 ÷ $5 gives 199 shares. That position is worth $9,950, or 9.95% of the account, which is under the 15% cap, so risk is the binding limit. If the stop is hit, the loss is 199 × $5 + $5 = $1,000. With a $60 target the trade offers $10 of upside for $5 of downside, a 2 : 1 reward-to-risk ratio.

Move the stop up to $49.50 and the risk per share falls to $0.50. The risk math would now allow 1,990 shares, worth almost $100,000, but the 15% cap limits the trade to 300 shares. The loss at the stop drops to $155, because the cap, not the risk budget, is now in control.

Why the stop comes first

The stop-loss should come from the chart or your trading plan, such as a level below recent support or a multiple of the stock's average daily range. Set it first, then let the calculator find the size. Moving the stop closer just to buy more shares tends to get you stopped out by ordinary price swings.

The table assumes each loss is a fixed share of the account as it stands after the previous loss. Small risk percentages keep a losing streak survivable.

Limits of this estimate

  • A stop-loss is not guaranteed. If a stock gaps past your stop, for example overnight or after earnings, the loss can be larger than planned.
  • The calculator assumes whole shares and ignores margin requirements, borrowing costs on short sales and taxes.
  • It sizes one trade at a time. Several open positions in related stocks can add up to more risk than any single trade shows.

faq.question: What percentage of my account should I risk on one trade?
faq.answer: There is no single correct figure, but many active traders keep it between 0.5% and 2% of the account. A lower figure means smaller swings in your balance and a better chance of surviving a run of losing trades.

faq.question: What is the difference between risk per trade and maximum position size?
faq.answer: Risk per trade limits how much you can lose if the stop-loss is hit. Maximum position size limits how much money goes into the stock in the first place. With a very tight stop, the risk limit alone could allow a huge position, so the cap keeps any single holding from dominating the account.

faq.question: Why is the loss at the stop slightly lower than my risk budget?
faq.answer: Shares are rounded down to a whole number so the loss never exceeds your budget. The leftover amount is usually less than the price risk on one share.

faq.question: Can I use this calculator for short selling?
faq.answer: Yes. Choose the short direction and enter a stop-loss above your entry price. The maths is the same, but short sales can also carry borrowing fees and margin requirements that this calculator does not include.

faq.question: What does the reward-to-risk ratio tell me?
faq.answer: It compares the distance from entry to your profit target with the distance from entry to your stop. A ratio of 2 : 1 means the planned gain is twice the planned loss, so the trade can be worthwhile even if fewer than half of such trades succeed.

faq.question: Is my information stored or sent anywhere?
faq.answer: No. The calculation runs entirely in your browser, and nothing you enter is sent to a server or saved.
